result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.random_reference()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Build a random reference graph with the same degrees (degree-preserving rewiring). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L28038-L28101){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.random_reference( niter=1, connectivity=True, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Random reference graph](/assets/graphs/random-reference.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: an eight-node ring with four chords that close four triangles, average clustering 0.667. Right: random_reference(seed=8) rewires it with degree-preserving swaps: the four accent edges on the left are replaced by the four accent edges on the right, every node keeps its degree (4 or 2), and the triangles mostly disappear, leaving an average clustering of 0.229." width="100%"} The result keeps every node's degree but scrambles the wiring with random double edge swaps (`a-b, c-d` becomes `a-d, c-b`), destroying structure such as clustering and communities. Comparing a network with such references tells whether a property (high clustering, short paths, motifs) is more than a consequence of the degree sequence. It is the random baseline of `small_world_sigma()` and `small_world_omega()`. The graph is treated as undirected and simple (parallel edges and self-loops are dropped). With `connectivity=True`, swaps that would disconnect the graph are undone. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [niter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Rewiring rounds, each attempting one swap per edge (default 1). [connectivity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), keep the graph connected. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducible results. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected, unweighted graph with the same nodes (IDs, labels and attributes kept) and rewired edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or has fewer than four nodes or two edges. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Follows NetworkX's `random_reference` (Maslov and Sneppen, 2002): endpoints are drawn with probability proportional to degree, then a random neighbor of each; the swap is applied when the four nodes are distinct and the new edges do not exist, and undone if it disconnects the first pair. Each round makes up to $2E/(V-1)$ attempts per edge. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Rewiring keeps the degrees and the connectivity: ::: {#296f951d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=30, k=4, p=0.1, seed=1) r = g.random_reference(niter=5, seed=2) def degree_sequence(graph): return sorted(graph.get_degree(n) for n in graph.get_node_ids(limit=None)) degree_sequence(g) == degree_sequence(r), r.is_connected() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, True) ``` ::: :::
